title: Redwood cost/econ discovery - Axiom Capital
summary: Discovery focused on per-token unit economics across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Axiom currently doing ~200M tokens/mo for a portfolio of analyst-assist features. Key takeaways: hosted is easiest to start but unit cost is higher; Dedicated reduces unit cost with a commit but requires commit/forecast and some infra work; Private gives best cost/controls for strict compliance but longer ops lead time. Caching (prefix + KV) and batching recommendations could reduce effective token spend by ~30-50% depending on prompt reuse. Next steps: Alex to send pricing tier sheet, Priya to share batching/caching whitepaper + benchmark link, schedule a dedicated cost-benchmark run on sample workload.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private economics
next_steps: Alex Chen: Send detailed pricing spreadsheet and example unit-econ model by 2026-03-06
Priya Nair: Share batching/caching guide and benchmark link by 2026-03-05
Schedule pilot benchmark (1 week run) w/ Axiom sample prompts - target week of 2026-03-16
action_items: Alex Chen: Prepare pricing + 3 scenarios (self-serve hosted, 6-mo dedicated commit, private on-prem estimate) - due 2026-03-06
Priya Nair: Run quick perf/cost sim using Axiom sample (expected 200M tokens/mo) and share results - due 2026-03-09
Liam O'Reilly: Provide final prompt corpus (anonymized) and SLA constraints - due 2026-03-10
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, Alex from Redwood here. Thanks for joining, happy to kick off.
[00:06] Sofia Martinez: Hi Alex, thanks. We pulled Liam and Noah in, we wanted to focus today on unit economics - we've got budget constraints across Q2/Q3 so want to understand hosted vs dedicated cost math.
[00:15] Priya Nair: Hi all, Priya from Redwood infra/SE, I can dive into batching and caching levers.
[00:23] Liam O'Reilly: Quick context: Axiom runs an analyst-assist product that synths research notes, average exchange length is ~280 tokens output, 90 tokens prompt on average; traffic pattern spiky around earnings windows. Goal is keep median latency <750ms tail 95 <1.5s.
[00:42] Alex Chen: Great, that's helpful. Rough numbers we usually use: hosted is easiest to start with no commit and predictable dev time, but per-token unit is higher; Dedicated with a commit drops the per-token effective cost quite a bit, and Private can be lower still but ops cost higher. We'll walk through numbers.
[00:57] Sofia Martinez: We estimate about 200M tokens a month across features. Curious what that maps to in dollars.
[01:04] Priya Nair: Right, so for a worked example: with our standard hosted model profile for this class of model, the list per-token rate we use for estimation is around $0.00025 per token for generation. That yields about $50k/month raw token spend at 200M tokens, note that's a ballpark.
[01:28] Noah Patel: Sorry, did you say quarter? 50k per month?
[01:31] Priya Nair: Yeah, 200M * 0.00025 = $50,000. Again that's raw model cost; there are also request/ingress egress and storage but those are smaller.
[01:40] Liam O'Reilly: That's higher than our expectations. How does dedicated change that?
[01:44] Alex Chen: With dedicated reserved capacity we can usually bring effective per-token to ~0.00008/token range depending on commit and instance mix - example math: same 200M tokens becomes ~16k in nominal model compute cost? (note: rhetorical), sorry, becomes about $16,000/month model compute for the committed tier.
[02:04] Sofia Martinez: I want to be careful - you said 0.00008, that's less than a third of hosted - what drives that delta?
[02:10] Priya Nair: Two things: reserved capacity gives us the leverage to allocate GPUs more fully and pass through lower execution cost; second is we can optimize kernel selection and packing for persistent workloads; batching and KV/prefix caching also reduce the number of tokens we actually execute.
[02:25] Liam O'Reilly: Can you quantify caching impact? We have a lot of repeated context - templates, standard corp summaries.
[02:32] Priya Nair: Yeah typical prefix or template reuse can reduce computed tokens by 20-50% depending on reuse. For example if you prefix 120 tokens that are identical for many requests, we only need to send/store once in KV cache so effective model tokens drop. In Axiom's case if you see 40% reuse across the 280-token outputs, that's a big reduction.
[02:50] Noah Patel: How does that work with stateful sessions? We do interactive sessions with analysts.
[02:54] Priya Nair: We support per-session KV caching; the runtime maintains KV cache so repeated prefixes or earlier conversation state doesn't re-run full attention. There are some limits (cache TTLs, memory) and it depends on sequence length distribution. We'll share our KV cache guide.
[03:07] Sofia Martinez: What about batching? We can't add too much latency.
[03:10] Priya Nair: Right - continuous batching helps improve GPU utilization. Small micro-batches (e.g., 4-8 requests) can yield cost improvements of 15-30% without hurting median latency much; aggressive batching (pushing to 50-100) helps throughput at the cost of tail latency. For your 750ms median target, we think a conservative batching policy could shave ~20% off effective cost.
[03:30] Alex Chen: So if you combine caching and conservative batching you can expect 30-45% lower effective model spend than raw per-token math. That moves hosted from $50k to maybe ~$28-35k; dedicated then after commit and the same levers could be ~$9-12k.
[03:46] Liam O'Reilly: Ok that delta looks attractive. What's the tradeoff? Lock-in? SLA?
[03:50] Alex Chen: Dedicated requires a commit (6 or 12 months typical) and some setup - e.g., capacity planning and routing. You get SLOs and capacity isolation. Private (VPC/on-prem) is more work: longer lead time and ops overhead, but better control over costs and compliance. We can provide an ops package if you want us to manage.
[04:05] Sofia Martinez: Do you have a worked example we can run with our prompts? A benchmark?
[04:09] Priya Nair: Yes, we typically run a 1-week pilot with sample prompt corpus - we can instrument token counts, latency percentiles, and show the realized cost with our caching/batching config. We'll also compare hosted vs dedicated for the same traffic profile.
[04:20] Liam O'Reilly: What's the minimum commit for dedicated?
[04:23] Alex Chen: We typically structure committed tiers with a monthly reserved spend that maps to GPU-hours. Minimums vary but for your expected 200M tokens/month we'd look at a mid-tier commitment; I'll include concrete numbers in the pricing sheet.
[04:34] Noah Patel: Security/regulatory - can you confirm data retention and KMS? We need to keep notes for audits and we have strict KMS requirements.
[04:41] Alex Chen: Yes, Hosted supports customer-managed KMS for keys in the Dedicated and Private offerings; we provide audit logs and SOC 2 documentation. For Private on-prem you control the keys fully. I'll share our security pack.
[04:52] Sofia Martinez: If we did hosted to start and then move to dedicated later, what's the migration risk?
[04:57] Priya Nair: We built the platform so the API and model pins are consistent across deployment modes. Migration is mostly capacity/config. There may be small perf differences depending on instance types, but fallbacks exist. We've migrated other customers within a few weeks.
[05:10] Liam O'Reilly: For budgeting, we have a monthly runaway cap of $40k for proof-of-concept. Sounds like hosted without caching might exceed that, but with caching/batching maybe it fits.
[05:19] Alex Chen: Exactly - our recommended path: start with Hosted plus aggressive caching and conservative batching to validate, run the 1-week benchmark to project actual spend, then evaluate Dedicated commit if host costs are high. We'll illustrate three scenarios in the sheet (no caching, caching+batches, dedicated commit).
[05:33] Sofia Martinez: Any gotchas on token counting? We saw differences between vendors.
[05:36] Priya Nair: Tokenization differences happen; we use a consistent tokenizer per model profile. For budgeting we run the sample corpus through our tokenizer to get accurate counts which we'll include in the benchmark.
[05:45] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[05:48] Noah Patel: On the benchmarks - can you also include tail latency at 95/99 and suggestions for autoscale? We want to avoid dropped queries.
[05:54] Priya Nair: Yes typical autoscale uses threshold-based policy plus burst buckets; we can suggest a policy that keeps 95th under your target while allowing bursts to use spot/burst capacity. We'll include recommended autoscale knobs.
[06:07] Liam O'Reilly: How do you handle model quantization and perf tradeoffs? We might tolerate slight quality loss for big cost wins.
[06:13] Priya Nair: We have quantization profiles and can recommend model variants; for many workloads int8 or Q4 quant gets you 2-3x throughput improvements with minor quality impact. We'll run quality regression checks against your eval set.
[06:25] Alex Chen: I'll also attach a simple spreadsheet showing sensitivity: tokens per request, reuse %, batch size - and how it maps to monthly cost and latency.
[06:33] Sofia Martinez: That would be helpful. If the pilot shows we can hit $25k or less, we can commit to a 6-month dedicated.
[06:40] Alex Chen: Great - that's actionable. Any other constraints?
[06:43] Noah Patel: Data residency - some EU data must stay in EU region. Is that supported?
[06:47] Alex Chen: Yes regional routing and private deployments in EU are supported; for Hosted we have EU regions and Dedicated/Private can be colocated. We'll note that in the docs.
[06:56] Liam O'Reilly: Any competitors we should watch? We tested with CloudEndpoints and had issues with caching/consistency.
[07:02] Alex Chen: We hear that - our differentiators are runtime caching, unified API, and cost controls. But we'll outline tradeoffs versus Anthropic/OpenAI staples in the appendix.
[07:12] Sofia Martinez: Cool. Quick question - do you charge for KV cache storage?
[07:16] Priya Nair: Minimal storage fees; the main cost is compute. For dedicated/private, KV resides in memory on the serving tier, so it's included in committed price; for hosted there are small storage + retrieval fees but usually negligible relative to token compute.
[07:31] Liam O'Reilly: Can you email an example bill reconciliation? We need to show finance how we'd forecast.
[07:36] Alex Chen: Yes, included in deliverables - a forecast template with sensitivity bands.
[07:40] Speaker 2: (brief crosstalk)
[07:44] Sofia Martinez: Ok last item - timeline. We want to decide on pilot by next week and run it mid-March.
[07:50] Alex Chen: We'll aim to get the pilot scheduled week of 2026-03-16; I'll send the pricing and pilot instructions by Friday.
[07:57] Priya Nair: I'll upload the batching/caching guide and a short runbook for the pilot. Link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/axiom-pilot (placeholder).
[08:06] Liam O'Reilly: Thanks all.
[08:08] Alex Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and next steps.
[08:11] (call ends)

Notes: transcription has occasional mislabels (Speaker 1/2) and minor fill words omitted - original Fireflies export. Links to security docs and pricing sheet will be shared via email.
